Addiction to alcohol

A randomized active-comparator trial reduced short-term craving and AUDIT scores in people with subclinical alcohol use. An older uncontrolled study reported mood and beta-endorphin changes, but not abstinence or relapse.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A randomized active-comparator trial reduced short-term craving and AUDIT scores in people with subclinical alcohol use. An older uncontrolled study reported mood and beta-endorphin changes, but not abstinence or relapse.

Summary of the Evidence

Two human publications directly examined alcohol addiction or subclinical alcohol use: one randomized active-comparator trial and one uncontrolled adjunct-treatment study. A separate mouse publication was mapped from alcohol-related cognitive impairment; it tested learning and brain-tissue outcomes after chronic alcohol exposure, not treatment of addiction or dependence. No in-vitro or ex-vivo study directly addressing alcohol addiction was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In a 2026 randomized trial, 60 people with subclinical alcohol use received transcranial PBM, transauricular vagus-nerve stimulation (taVNS), or both for five weeks. PBM alone and the combined intervention reduced craving scores and AUDIT alcohol-use scores more than taVNS alone. The study had no sham-PBM or usual-care group, and its participants were not a treatment-seeking alcohol-dependence cohort (Kwon et al. 2026).

An older single-arm study followed 53 people receiving laser biostimulation alongside laser auricular acupuncture. Depression scores decreased and beta-endorphin levels increased, but the study did not establish abstinence, reduced relapse, or a comparative treatment effect (Zalewska-Kaszubska and Obzejta 2004).

Animal evidence

A mouse model of adolescent chronic alcohol exposure reported improved cognitive and spatial-memory performance and reduced hippocampal reactive gliosis after PBM. This is related evidence about alcohol-associated brain changes; it does not test craving, dependence, withdrawal, or relapse (Hong et al. 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly examining PBM for alcohol addiction was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The recent trial used an 850-nm near-infrared LED device over 19 scalp channels, for 15 minutes per session, five times weekly for five weeks. It tested 10-, 15-, and 18-Hz pulsed settings, but did not report a light dose. The older combined laser protocol used 514-nm visible green and 633-nm visible red light, with neck and ear-point delivery. The mapped mouse study used 830-nm near-infrared light. These routes and populations differ, and the available work does not identify a common dose or clinical treatment schedule.

Interpretation

The randomized study found short-term craving and questionnaire-score reductions relative to taVNS alone in a subclinical-use sample. The older report found mood and biomarker changes without measuring abstinence or relapse. The mouse findings concern alcohol-related cognition rather than addiction treatment. Whether PBM reduces alcohol consumption, supports treatment retention, or prevents relapse in people with alcohol dependence remains untested in controlled clinical trials.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term craving reduction in subclinical alcohol use Very low for alcohol-dependence treatment or relapse prevention
Publications and records2 direct human publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The randomized study reduced craving and AUDIT scores compared with taVNS alone, but participants had subclinical alcohol use and there was no sham or usual-care group. The older single-arm study measured mood and beta-endorphin, not abstinence or relapse. Trials in treatment-seeking patients with blinded controls, drinking outcomes, retention, adverse events, and longer follow-up are needed.
